clue.text: Utterly baffling — one bull is slaughtered

indicators.note: the bull being slaughtered means the letters of these three words are hacked apart and reassembled

explanation.surface: A matador's bewildering afternoon: a bull is killed and nobody can explain why.
explanation.walkthrough: 'is' belongs to the fodder, not the link: ONE BULL IS has exactly the nine letters needed.
explanation.definitionFit: A problem that cannot be solved at all is utterly baffling.

clue.text: Yet I repeatedly climb when injured? It's sheer stupidity!

indicators.note: an injured body is twisted out of shape, so the fodder letters are rearranged

parts.note: taken as written

indicators.note: the single letter I is to be used more than once, here twice

parts.note: the letter I, taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A climber keeps going up even when hurt, and the speaker calls it plain foolishness.
explanation.walkthrough: 'when injured' rearranges YET, II (I 'repeatedly') and CLIMB together, ten letters with three Is in all.
explanation.definitionFit: Imbecility is extreme foolishness, the quality of an idiot.

clue.text: Cops, we hear, finding nine shot, ambushed by foreign agent

definitions.note: the words sound like copse, a small wood

indicators.note: to be ambushed is to be surrounded, so the agent's letters enclose the others

parts.note: a foreign agent is a spy

indicators.note: shot is used in its sense of ruined or broken, so the letters of nine are scrambled

explanation.surface: Police officers stumble on nine bodies, gunned down in an ambush by an enemy spy.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition is itself a sound-alike: 'Cops, we hear' gives COPSE, a small wood. 'shot' makes INNE, which 'ambushed by' encloses.
explanation.definitionFit: A spinney is a small thicket of trees, which is exactly what a copse is.

clue.text: Unusually early to bed

indicators.note: done unusually means not in the normal order, so the letters of early are rearranged

explanation.surface: Someone is turning in for the night earlier than usual.
explanation.walkthrough: 'bed' looks like the place to sleep, but it is the geologist's bed, a stratum.
explanation.definitionFit: A bed of rock or soil is a stratum, one level in a stack of deposits.

clue.text: Maybe heading for heart of ship historic Irish adventurer's taken over

indicators.note: in a down entry, something taken over the other is placed above it, so it comes first

parts.note: Colonel Thomas Blood was the 17th-century Irish adventurer who tried to steal the Crown Jewels
a ship is a vessel

explanation.surface: A tale of a sea adventurer seizing a ship and steering it for home.
explanation.walkthrough: 'taken over' sets the adventurer on top in this down entry. Colonel Blood is famous in Britain for his 1671 attempt on the Crown Jewels in the Tower of London.
explanation.definitionFit: A vein is one kind of blood vessel, carrying blood back towards the heart, hence 'maybe'.

clue.text: Oculus — the yellow part

explanation.surface: A Latin term for an organ of sight sits beside a description of something golden.
explanation.definitionFit: Oculus is Latin for the organ of sight; a flower such as a daisy has a yellow centre called its eye.

clue.text: Start eating in a buffet, but it's second-rate

indicators.note: one piece is placed inside another, as the clue says the start of eating goes in the buffet

parts.note: a buffet is a heavy knock, a blow

indicators.note: the start of the word eating is its opening letter

explanation.surface: A diner begins on the food at a buffet but finds the spread mediocre.
explanation.walkthrough: 'buffet' reads as a spread of food, but here it is a blow. 'in' puts E, the start of 'eating', inside BLOW.
explanation.definitionFit: Work that falls below standard is inferior, that is second-rate.

clue.text: Poor Bernie, with three daughters laid up

indicators.note: poor in the sense of badly made, so the letters are put together differently

parts.note: taken as written
D is the usual abbreviation for daughter, so three of them give three Ds

explanation.surface: Unlucky Bernie, father of three girls, is stuck in bed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Poor' rearranges BERNIE together with DDD, the three daughters.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone confined to bed by illness is said to be laid up.

clue.text: Disciple of the French finding English composer first-rate

parts.note: le is French for the
Thomas Arne, the English composer of Rule, Britannia!

indicators.note: joined to rate as first-rate, it asks for the opening letter of that word

explanation.surface: A follower of a Frenchman finds an English composer outstanding.
explanation.walkthrough: 'first-rate' looks like praise, but it means only the first letter of 'rate', R. Thomas Arne wrote Rule, Britannia!
explanation.definitionFit: A disciple is a pupil or student of a master, someone who is still being taught.

clue.text: Stick pale daughter needed

parts.note: wan means pale

explanation.surface: A father insists on keeping his sickly-looking daughter at home.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Stick' looks like a verb but is the noun, a thin rod.
explanation.definitionFit: A wand is a slender rod, such as a conductor's baton or a magician's stick.

clue.text: The main skating area Kelvin avoided by going outside

indicators.note: the word by goes outside, wrapping round the other letters

parts.note: taken as written

indicators.note: kelvin is avoided, meaning its letter is left out of the skating area

parts.note: a rink is an area for skating
K is the symbol for the kelvin, the unit of temperature

explanation.surface: A skater called Kelvin heads outdoors rather than use the indoor rink.
explanation.walkthrough: 'avoided' leaves RIN once Kelvin is dropped, and 'going outside' wraps the word 'by' round it. 'The main' is an old phrase for the open sea.
explanation.definitionFit: The briny is a jokey name for the sea, from the salt water.

clue.text: Exaggerated and is no longer credited

explanation.surface: Someone whose story was over the top now finds that people no longer believe them.
explanation.definitionFit: An overdrawn portrait or account is exaggerated; an overdrawn bank account has gone into debit, no longer in credit.

clue.text: Accord not in it, in one word

definitions.text: Accord not in it, in one word

indicators.note: the four words are to be remade as a single word, so their letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: A grammar puzzle: express the idea of no agreement using just one word.
explanation.walkthrough: The four words before the comma rearrange into the answer, and the whole clue also defines it: a contradiction is a statement with no agreement within it.
explanation.definitionFit: A contradiction is a statement whose parts disagree, so there is no harmony inside it.

clue.text: Favour an appearance

explanation.surface: Two words a stage manager might use: to back an act, and to show up.
explanation.definitionFit: To countenance something is to support or approve it; a countenance is a face, a person's look or appearance.

clue.text: Art-deco rug, extraordinarily groovy

indicators.note: extraordinary means out of the ordinary, so the letters are taken out of their order

explanation.surface: An Art Deco rug is praised as wonderfully cool.
explanation.walkthrough: 'groovy' looks like 1960s slang for cool, but it is literal: full of grooves.
explanation.definitionFit: Corrugated sheet has parallel ridges and furrows along it, literally covered in grooves.

clue.text: Delayed going round, however, to small outfit

indicators.note: the first word's letters go round the second, enclosing it

parts.note: delayed means late
yet can mean however, as in yet it moves

explanation.surface: Someone held up nonetheless makes it to a little firm.
explanation.walkthrough: 'outfit' suggests a company, but it means clothes; 'going round' sets 'however' within 'delayed'.
explanation.definitionFit: A layette is the set of clothes and bedding prepared for a newborn baby, an outfit for someone small.

clue.text: Signal when obstruction comes to light -for example knock hard!

indicators.note: coming to light means rising, so in this down entry the word is written upwards

parts.note: let is an old word for a hindrance, as in without let or hindrance
to rap is to knock
H stands for hard, as on pencils

explanation.surface: Somebody hammers at a blockage when it is uncovered, as if sending a message.
explanation.walkthrough: 'comes to light' is a rising in this down entry, turning LET into TEL. LET as an obstruction survives in the phrase 'without let or hindrance' and in tennis.
explanation.definitionFit: To telegraph is to send a message by wire, or to give a signal of an intention in advance.

clue.text: Suffer, having to travel by tube

explanation.surface: A commuter who goes by Underground complains of the ordeal.
explanation.walkthrough: The second sense splits the answer into two words: to travel by tube is to go under the streets.
explanation.definitionFit: To go through hardship is to suffer it; taking the London Underground (the tube) means going beneath the city.

clue.text: Cerebral shrines?

parts.note: places of worship that belong to the head, read as the flat sides of the skull beside the brain

explanation.surface: Seemingly holy places devoted to the intellect.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark flags a play: the same word means places of worship and the sides of the forehead.
explanation.definitionFit: Shrines are places of worship, and the same word names the flat parts of the head beside the eyes.

clue.text: Bogus uprising squeezes out these drivers

indicators.note: one part squeezes the other, holding it tightly inside
in a down entry something rising is read from bottom to top

parts.note: bogus means sham, fake
taken as written

explanation.surface: A fake rebellion forces out a group of chauffeurs.
explanation.walkthrough: 'uprising' looks like a revolt, but it turns the fake upwards to MAHS, which 'squeezes' the word 'out' in its middle.
explanation.definitionFit: A mahout is a person who drives and tends an elephant, chiefly in South Asia.

clue.text: More pungent port

explanation.surface: A sharper flavour, and a harbour city.
explanation.definitionFit: Tangier is the comparative of tangy, sharper in flavour; Tangier is also the Moroccan port on the Strait of Gibraltar.

clue.text: I travel with a student — one or Iris's family

parts.note: taken as written
to ride is to travel
L, for learner, stands for a student, as on L-plates

explanation.surface: Someone sets off with a pupil, the pair being related to a woman named Iris.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Iris' looks like a woman's name, but it is the plant. L is the learner on British L-plates.
explanation.definitionFit: Irideal is a botanical term for a member of the plant group that contains the irises.

clue.text: Tossing the caber for example?

parts.note: a throw at the Scottish Games, read literally as a hurling done in the northern hills

explanation.surface: A question about Scottish strongman events.
explanation.walkthrough: The Highland fling is a Scottish dance, but read literally it is a throw in the Highlands, such as tossing the caber, a heavy pole hurled at Scottish Games.
explanation.definitionFit: A throw is a fling, and caber-tossing is a Scottish Highlands sport.

clue.text: Growing girl?

parts.note: a girl's name that also covers all that grows in a region, its plant life

explanation.surface: A young lass shooting up fast.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark flags that 'Growing' means plant life, not a child getting taller.
explanation.definitionFit: The word is a woman's name and also the plant life of a place, everything that grows there.

clue.text: Basket you get in spring

explanation.surface: A wicker basket of the kind used to bring in the spring harvest.
explanation.walkthrough: 'spring' looks like the season, but it means a jump. The basket sense is an old dialect word, often for a fish trap.
explanation.definitionFit: A leap in old and dialect English is a wicker basket or fish trap; a spring is a jump.

clue.text: Cautioned about instruction

indicators.note: about means turned round or moved around, so the letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: A warning has been given concerning the orders.
explanation.walkthrough: 'about' looks like 'concerning', but it rearranges CAUTIONED.
explanation.definitionFit: Education is teaching, the giving of instruction.

clue.text: I am obtaining piano for the little chap

parts.note: I am shortens to I'm
P stands for piano, softly, in music

explanation.surface: Someone claims to be getting hold of a piano for a small boy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'obtaining' simply joins I'M to P, which follows it. P is the musical mark for soft.
explanation.definitionFit: An imp is a little devil, and a mischievous child is called a little imp.

clue.text: Patent ring with heraldic colouring

parts.note: a ring is shaped like the letter O
vert is the heraldic word for green

explanation.surface: A design for a ring with coloured enamel is registered with the patent office.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Patent' looks like the legal protection, but it is the adjective, obvious.
explanation.definitionFit: Something patent is plain to see, openly shown and not hidden.

clue.text: Easter — and father's going to church

parts.note: pa is father, with the possessive s

explanation.surface: Dad heads to church for the Easter service.
explanation.walkthrough: Pasch is an old word for Easter or the Passover, from Greek pascha.
explanation.definitionFit: Pasch, from the Hebrew for Passover, is an old name for the Easter festival.

clue.text: Quiet clergyman was unwell but had his way

parts.note: P is the musical mark piano, meaning quiet
Rev, Reverend, is a clergyman's title
ailed means was unwell

explanation.surface: A soft-spoken vicar fell ill but still got what he wanted.
explanation.walkthrough: P is piano, the musical mark for quiet.
explanation.definitionFit: To win through over opposition is to prevail, getting one's own way.
